questions.stem: Sally, 47, is lying still on the ED trolley. She has had constant right upper quadrant pain for 26 hours and is febrile. You are examining her abdomen and want to elicit Murphy's sign, telling the examiner what you are doing. How do you perform the manoeuvre?
options: Press deeply in the right upper quadrant, then let go quickly and watch for pain
Press in the left iliac fossa and ask whether she feels pain referred to the right side
Press under right costal margin at the midclavicular line as she inhales deeply
Lay a hand over the lower right ribs and strike it firmly with the other fist
questions.why: Murphy's sign: fingers under the right costal margin at the midclavicular line (gallbladder fundus), then deep inspiration. It is positive if she stops breathing in because of pain as the inflamed gallbladder descends onto your fingers. Repeat it on the left, where it should be negative.
notes: This is rebound tenderness, a general sign of peritoneal irritation; it does not test the gallbladder's descent on inspiration and is needlessly painful.
This is Rovsing's sign for appendicitis, and Sally has already had an appendicectomy.
Fist percussion tests renal angle or liver tenderness; it does not look for the catch in inspiration that defines Murphy's sign.

questions.stem: Sally, 47, has acute calculous cholecystitis on ultrasound. T 38.9 °C, HR 108, BP 122/74, normal lactate and renal function, no known drug allergies, BMI 32. Blood cultures have been taken and she is being admitted under general surgery. Which empirical antibiotic regimen does eTG recommend now?
options: Amoxicillin 2 g IV 6-hourly plus gentamicin 4 to 7 mg/kg IV as a single dose
Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg orally 12-hourly, then discharge to clinic
Vancomycin 25 mg/kg IV loading dose plus metronidazole 500 mg IV 12-hourly
Meropenem 1 g IV 8-hourly as monotherapy until the culture results return
questions.why: For acute cholecystitis eTG recommends IV amoxicillin 2 g 6-hourly plus gentamicin 4 to 7 mg/kg (adjusted body weight if obese), with later doses timed by renal function. Ceftriaxone is the alternative if gentamicin is contraindicated.
notes: A febrile, tachycardic patient with acute cholecystitis needs admission, IV antibiotics and early cholecystectomy. This is not a discharge diagnosis.
Vancomycin targets Gram-positive organisms such as MRSA. It misses the Gram-negative enteric organisms that cause biliary infection, so it is not indicated here.
Meropenem is kept for known or suspected resistant organisms such as ESBL producers. Using it first line in community-acquired mild cholecystitis promotes resistance.

questions.stem: Sally, 47, says her pain began about 3 hours after a big fatty barbecue lunch. Over the past year she has had milder episodes in the same place after meals. Ultrasound now shows a 15 mm stone impacted in the gallbladder neck. Which mechanism best explains why fatty meals bring on her pain?
options: Secretin from duodenal S cells makes the gallbladder contract against the impacted stone
Gastrin from antral G cells makes the gallbladder contract against the impacted stone
Motilin from duodenal M cells makes the gallbladder contract against the impacted stone
Cholecystokinin from duodenal I cells makes the gallbladder contract against the stone
questions.why: Fat and amino acids in the duodenum release cholecystokinin from I cells. CCK contracts the gallbladder and relaxes the sphincter of Oddi, so the gallbladder squeezes against a stone blocking its neck or the cystic duct, which causes pain.
notes: Secretin is released in response to duodenal acid and mainly drives bicarbonate-rich pancreatic and biliary ductal secretion, not gallbladder contraction after fat.
Gastrin is released by peptides and gastric distension and mainly stimulates gastric acid secretion; it is not the main trigger for gallbladder contraction after fat.
Motilin drives the migrating motor complex in the fasting state; it is not released by a fatty meal.

questions.stem: When asked directly, Sally, 47, says she also has pain at the tip of her right shoulder. Ultrasound shows a distended, inflamed gallbladder with a rim of pericholecystic fluid, and she has a positive Murphy's sign. Which nerve pathway best explains the shoulder-tip pain?
options: Greater splanchnic nerve (T5 to T9) carrying visceral afferents from the gallbladder
Phrenic nerve (C3 to C5) from irritated diaphragmatic peritoneum, sharing C4 skin
Right vagus nerve carrying afferent fibres from the inflamed gallbladder wall
Lower intercostal nerves (T7 to T11) supplying the parietal peritoneum of the RUQ
questions.why: Inflammation spreading to the peritoneum under the diaphragm irritates phrenic nerve (C3 to C5) sensory fibres. The brain refers this pain to the shoulder tip, whose skin is supplied by the same segments (C3 to C4, supraclavicular nerves).
notes: Splanchnic visceral afferents cause the vague epigastric or RUQ pain of biliary colic, sometimes felt near the inferior angle of the scapula, but not at the shoulder tip.
Vagal afferents mainly carry non-painful sensation and reflexes such as nausea; they do not cause referred somatic pain at the shoulder.
Intercostal nerves supply the anterior abdominal parietal peritoneum and cause localised RUQ tenderness (as in Murphy's sign), not pain referred to the shoulder.
